subject: nlp
title: Label the diagram
description: Original numbered practice diagrams for Lectures 1–10, based on the course notes and slides. Pick the right label for each number. These are unofficial study reconstructions, not lecturer-authored diagrams.

questions.question: Label the parts of the Transformer architecture marked 1–9.

image.alt: The Transformer (encoder on the left, decoder on the right) with nine component labels hidden and numbered 1–9.

questions.explanation: Bottom up. Encoder (left): input embedding + positional encoding → [multi-head self-attention → add & norm → feed forward → add & norm] $\times N$. Decoder (right): output embedding + positional encoding → masked multi-head self-attention → add & norm → multi-head encoder–decoder (cross) attention, where Q comes from the decoder and K, V from the encoder → add & norm → feed forward → add & norm, $\times N$ → linear → softmax over the vocabulary.

questions.question: Label the seq2seq (encoder–decoder) pipeline marked 1–7.

image.alt: Seq2seq encoder–decoder pipeline with seven labels hidden and numbered 1–7.

labels.answer: h: vector representation of the context (source and previous history)
Previous history (target tokens generated so far)

options: h: vector representation of the context (source and previous history)
Previous history (target tokens generated so far)
questions.explanation: The encoder reads the source; the decoder reads the previous target history and, conditioned on the encoder, produces h. A linear layer projects h from size d to |V| and softmax gives the distribution over the next token. It's a conditional language model.

questions.question: Label the high-level pipeline of a neural language model marked 1–7.

image.alt: High-level neural language model pipeline with seven labels hidden and numbered 1–7.

labels.answer: h: vector representation of the context
Get probability distribution for the next token

options: h: vector representation of the context
Get probability distribution for the next token
questions.explanation: Two halves: (1) process the context with a model-specific network (RNN, CNN…) into a d-sized vector h; (2) a model-agnostic part: a linear layer d → |V| and softmax give P(next token | context). Equivalently, take dot products of h with the output word embeddings.

questions.question: Label the simplest RNN encoder–decoder model marked 1–8.

image.alt: Simplest RNN encoder–decoder model with eight labels hidden and numbered 1–8.

labels.answer: Vector representation of the source – used as the initial decoder state

options: Vector representation of the source – used as the initial decoder state
questions.explanation: The encoder RNN starts from an initial state (e.g. zeros), reads the source embeddings, and its final state becomes the decoder's initial state. The decoder RNN reads <bos> + the target tokens (output embeddings) and predicts the next target token at each step. That single vector is the bottleneck attention fixes.

questions.question: Complete the taxonomy of transfer learning in NLP: label the nodes marked 1–6.

image.alt: Tree diagram 'A Taxonomy of Transfer Learning in NLP' with six node labels hidden and numbered 1–6; the grey hints are also hidden.

questions.explanation: Transductive: same task, labels only for the source → domain adaptation (different domains) or cross-lingual learning (different languages). Inductive: different tasks, labels for the target task → multi-task learning (tasks learned simultaneously) or sequential transfer learning (tasks learned sequentially: pretrain, then fine-tune).

questions.question: This is the character-level CNN that ELMo uses to build a word representation for 'kitten'. Label the parts marked 1–5.

image.alt: ELMo's character-level CNN with a highway block; five labels hidden and numbered 1–5.

questions.explanation: Characters → convolution (several filters over character n-grams) → global max-pooling over positions (fixed-size vector) → 2 highway blocks (gate $g = \sigma(Wx + b)$ mixes a linear transform with the input: $g \cdot \mathrm{Linear}(x) + (1 - g) \cdot x$) → a final linear projection. Because it works from characters, ELMo is open-vocabulary.

questions.question: Label the three components of the ELMo architecture marked 1–3.

image.alt: ELMo architecture with three labels hidden and numbered 1–3.

questions.explanation: ELMo: char-CNN + highway layers give a context-independent token representation; a 2-layer forward LSTM language model and a separate 2-layer backward LSTM LM read the sentence; the ELMo representation is a task-specific weighted sum ($\lambda_0, \lambda_1, \lambda_2$) of the layers. No self-attention.

questions.question: This diagram shows how LoRA changes a layer. Label the parts marked 1–4.

image.alt: LoRA diagram: input feeds a frozen weight block and a weight-update block whose outputs are added; four labels hidden and numbered 1–4.

labels.answer: ΔW: trainable weight update (low-rank, ΔW = BA)

options: ΔW: trainable weight update (low-rank, ΔW = BA)
questions.explanation: LoRA freezes $W_0$ and learns $\Delta W = BA$ with rank $r \ll d$, so $h = W_0 x + BAx$. After training, $BA$ can be merged into $W_0$, so unlike adapters there's no extra inference latency.

questions.question: Label the BERT input representation: the three embedding rows (1–3) and the special tokens (4–5).

image.alt: BERT input representation for '[CLS] my dog is cute [SEP] he likes play ##ing [SEP]' with row names and the special tokens hidden; labels 1–5.

questions.explanation: Each input vector = token embedding + segment (sentence A/B) embedding + position embedding. [CLS] starts the input, and its final vector is used for classification / NSP; [SEP] separates and ends the segments. '##ing' is a WordPiece subword.

questions.question: Label the adapter diagram: the components in the Transformer layer (1–2) and inside the adapter layer (3–5).

image.alt: Transformer layer with adapters (left) and the inside of an adapter layer (right); labels 1–5 hidden.

questions.explanation: Adapters are inserted after the attention and feed-forward sublayers; only adapters (and layer norms) are trained, everything else is frozen and shared across tasks. Inside: down-project to a small hidden size → nonlinearity → up-project, plus a residual connection (few parameters).

questions.question: Label the attention computation pipeline marked 1–6 (stages and the operations between them).

image.alt: Attention computation pipeline with the stage names and the operations between stages hidden; labels 1–6.

questions.explanation: Input: all encoder states $s_1, \ldots, s_m$ and one decoder state $h_t$ → scores $\mathrm{score}(h_t, s_k)$ → softmax → attention weights $a_k^{(t)}$ → weighted sum → attention output $c^{(t)} = \sum_k a_k^{(t)} s_k$, the source context for decoder step $t$.

questions.question: Name the three attention score functions marked 1–3.

image.alt: The three attention score functions with their names hidden; labels 1–3.

questions.explanation: Dot-product: $h_t^T s_k$. Bilinear: $h_t^T W s_k$ (learned $W$; $W = I$ gives the dot product). MLP (additive): $w_2^T \tanh(W_1[h_t, s_k])$. Bahdanau used MLP, Luong used bilinear.

questions.question: This is the Bahdanau attention model. Label the parts marked 1–5.

image.alt: Bahdanau attention model with five labels hidden and numbered 1–5.

labels.answer: Bidirectional encoder: concatenate states from forward and backward RNNs
Pass source context c(t) and previous decoder state h(t−1) to the next step

options: Bidirectional encoder: concatenate states from forward and backward RNNs
Pass source context c(t) and previous decoder state h(t−1) to the next step
Combine source context c(t) and decoder state h(t) to make a prediction
questions.explanation: Bahdanau: bidirectional encoder; attention uses the previous decoder state $h_{t-1}$; MLP score function; the context $c^{(t)}$ is fed into the next decoder step together with $h_{t-1}$.

questions.question: This is the Luong attention model. Label the parts marked 1–4.

image.alt: Luong attention model with four labels hidden and numbered 1–4.

labels.answer: Combine source context c(t) and decoder state h(t) to make a prediction

options: Combine source context c(t) and decoder state h(t) to make a prediction
Pass source context c(t) and previous decoder state h(t−1) to the next step
Bidirectional encoder: concatenate states from forward and backward RNNs
questions.explanation: Luong: unidirectional encoder; attention uses the current decoder state $h_t$; bilinear score function; then $\tilde{h}_t = \tanh(W_c[h_t, c^{(t)}])$ combines context and state to predict the next token.

questions.question: Label the four stages that turn text into a word–context association score.

image.alt: A four-stage co-occurrence and PPMI pipeline with blank boxes numbered 1–4.

questions.explanation: Choose a focal word, count nearby words within the stated window, store the counts by focal/context pair, then use PPMI to highlight stronger-than-chance associations. With window 1, cat and mat in the tutorial sentence never co-occur, so PPMI(cat, mat) is 0.

questions.question: Label the Word2Vec skip-gram path and its two ways to train context predictions.

image.alt: A centre word flows through an embedding and context scores, then branches to two training choices, numbered 1–5.

questions.explanation: Skip-gram starts from a centre word and predicts surrounding words. A full softmax scores the whole vocabulary; negative sampling instead distinguishes the true pair from a few sampled non-pairs with sigmoid decisions. Both train the word vectors.

questions.question: Label the five stages of a text CNN classifier.

image.alt: A five-stage text CNN from word vectors to class scores, with boxes numbered 1–5.

questions.explanation: Filters detect local phrases at every position. Their feature maps vary with sentence length; global pooling makes one fixed-size sentence vector, which the classifier turns into class probabilities.

questions.question: Label the BPE training stages and the result used to tokenize new words.

image.alt: A four-stage BPE flow from characters through pair counting and learned rules to a new tokenization, numbered 1–4.

questions.explanation: During training, repeatedly count adjacent pairs and merge the most frequent one, saving each merge in order. At inference, start from characters and apply those learned merges in order; do not recalculate pair frequencies on the new word.

questions.concept: Recursive synthetic training and model collapse
questions.question: Label the four stages in a simplified model-collapse feedback loop.

image.alt: A four-stage loop from human text to a trained model, generated text and a later model, numbered 1–4.

questions.explanation: If a new model repeatedly trains on earlier models' output, rare patterns can disappear and generated text becomes more uniform. A shift toward very low perplexity, with a long tail, is one sign; low perplexity here does not prove better language.

questions.question: Label the input, router, active experts and output mixture of an MoE layer.

image.alt: A token is routed through two active expert branches that rejoin at an output, with five numbered boxes.

questions.explanation: The router scores experts for this token and activates only the top few. Their outputs are mixed by router weights; unselected experts do no work for this token. The two expert boxes share one valid label.

questions.question: Label the offline document path and online question-answering path in RAG.

image.alt: A six-box RAG flow: three offline boxes on top and three online boxes below, numbered 1–6.

questions.explanation: Offline, split documents into passages, embed them and store them for search. Online, use the query to retrieve relevant passages, then give those passages to the generator so it can answer with citations. Updating the documents does not require retraining the language model.
